A1.text:
There is a girl. Her name is Ella. She has a big house. But her mother is dead.

Her father marries again. He marries a woman with two daughters. The woman is not kind. The two girls are not kind.

Ella's father dies. Now Ella has no mother. She has no father. She lives with the woman and the two girls.

The woman calls her Cinderella. Why? Because Ella sits by the fire. The ashes cover her dress. She is always dirty.

Cinderella works all day. She cooks food. She cleans the house. She washes clothes. The two girls do nothing. They sit and play. They laugh at Cinderella.

Cinderella has no nice clothes. She has no nice shoes. She sleeps in the kitchen by the fire. She eats small pieces of food.

One day, a letter comes to the house. The letter says: "The king has a son. The prince wants to marry. There is a ball. All the girls in the town must come. The prince will choose a wife."

The two girls are very happy. "We will go!" they say. "We will wear nice dresses! The prince will like us!"

They buy expensive dresses. They buy expensive shoes. They spend many days making themselves beautiful.

"Cinderella," says the woman. "You will stay here. You will make our dinner. You will clean the house. You cannot go to the ball."

Cinderella is sad. She wants to go to the ball. She wants to see the prince. But she cannot go.

The night of the ball comes. The two girls leave. Cinderella is alone. She sits by the fire. She cries.

"Why do you cry?" says a small voice.

Cinderella looks. A woman stands there. But this woman is not the woman from before. This woman is very beautiful. She has a magic stick.

"I am your godmother," says the woman. "I am your fairy godmother. Do not cry. You will go to the ball."

"But I have no dress," says Cinderella. "I have no shoes."

"Bring me a pumpkin," says the fairy godmother.

Cinderella brings a pumpkin. The fairy godmother waves her stick. The pumpkin becomes a beautiful coach. It is gold. It is very big.

"Now bring me mice," says the fairy godmother.

Cinderella brings six mice. The fairy godmother waves her stick. The mice become six white horses. They are beautiful.

"Now you," says the fairy godmother. "You need a dress."

She waves her stick. Cinderella's old dress becomes a beautiful ball gown. It is white and gold. It is the most beautiful dress in the world. Cinderella also has beautiful shoes. The shoes are made of glass.

"You look beautiful!" says the fairy godmother. "But remember. At midnight, the magic stops. Your coach becomes a pumpkin. Your horses become mice. Your dress becomes old rags. You must go home before midnight."

"I will remember," says Cinderella.

Cinderella goes to the ball. She sits in the beautiful coach. The horses run fast. Soon she arrives at the castle.

Everyone looks at her. They do not know who she is. The two girls do not know her. The prince sees her. He forgets about everyone else. He only looks at Cinderella.

"May I dance with you?" asks the prince.

"Yes," says Cinderella.

They dance together. They dance for a long time. Cinderella is happy.

Cinderella and the prince talk. They laugh together. The prince thinks she is wonderful. He forgets about everything else.

Suddenly, Cinderella hears the clock. It is midnight! The magic will stop!

Cinderella runs away. She runs down the stairs. One glass shoe falls off her foot. She leaves it on the stairs. She runs to the coach. She goes home.

The coach becomes a pumpkin. Her dress becomes old rags. But she still has one glass shoe.

The prince finds the glass shoe on the stairs. "I will find her," he says. "I will search the whole town. I will find the girl who fits this shoe. I will marry her."

The prince goes to every house in the town. He has the glass shoe. Every girl tries to put it on. But it does not fit anyone.

At last the prince comes to Cinderella's house. The two girls try. The shoe does not fit them.

"Does anyone else live here?" asks the prince.

"Only Cinderella," says the woman. "But she is just a servant. She is dirty."

"I want to see her," says the prince.

Cinderella comes down. She is wearing old rags. Her face is dirty. But the prince knows her. It is his beautiful dance partner!

Cinderella puts on the glass shoe. It fits perfectly.

The prince is very happy. "I have found you!" he says. "Will you marry me?"

"Yes," says Cinderella.

Cinderella and the prince marry. They are very happy. Cinderella goes to live in the castle. She is a princess now.

The fairy godmother is happy. Cinderella is happy. Everyone is happy. Even the two mean girls are sorry. They ask for forgiveness. Cinderella forgives them.

Cinderella lives in the castle with the prince. She has beautiful dresses. She has beautiful shoes. She has everything she wants. She is never sad again.

A2.text:
Long ago there lived a kind girl named Ella. She had everything a girl could want: a loving mother, a wealthy father, and a beautiful home. But one sad day, her mother became ill and died. A few years later, her father also died, leaving Ella alone in the world.

Certain that Ella needed a mother's care, her father's relatives found her a new mother. He married a widow who had two daughters of her own. However, this woman was not kind. She was cold and unkind. Her two daughters were just like her—mean and selfish.

After Ella's father's death, everything changed. The stepmother showed her true nature. She forced Ella to work as a servant in her own home. Ella cooked the meals, cleaned the house, and washed the clothes while her stepsisters sat idle, only concerned with their appearance and their pleasures.

Because Ella always sat by the fireplace, covered in ashes from the cooking fires, her stepsisters gave her a cruel nickname: "Cinderella." The name stuck, and soon everyone in the household called her by this name, forgetting her real name entirely.

Years passed, and Cinderella's life remained miserable. She slept in the kitchen, wore tattered clothes, and ate only scraps of food left over from meals. Yet despite her suffering, she remained kind-hearted and gentle.

One day, an announcement arrived at the house. The king had declared a grand ball to be held at the palace. The prince, now of age, would choose a bride from all the eligible young ladies in the kingdom. The stepmother and her two daughters became excited about this opportunity.

"I shall wear my best red velvet dress!" declared the elder stepsister.

"And I shall wear my finest yellow silk gown!" said the younger one, jealously.

The stepmother smiled wickedly. "And Cinderella, you shall prepare our hair and make us look beautiful. Then you shall stay home to prepare our supper."

Cinderella's heart sank. She wanted so desperately to attend the ball, to see the prince, to dance just once in her life. But she said nothing and did as she was told.

On the night of the ball, the stepmother and stepsisters left in their carriage. Cinderella sat alone in the kitchen, crying softly. Suddenly, a brilliant light filled the room, and an elegant woman appeared before her.

"Do not cry, my dear child," said the woman gently. "I am your fairy godmother. You shall go to the ball."

"But how?" asked Cinderella. "I have no dress, and the carriage is gone."

"Go to the garden," commanded the fairy godmother, "and bring me a pumpkin."

Cinderella obeyed. When she returned with a large pumpkin, the fairy godmother touched it with her wand, and it transformed into a magnificent golden coach.

"Now bring me six mice," said the fairy godmother.

When Cinderella brought the mice, the fairy godmother touched each one with her wand. They became six white horses, prancing and eager.

"Now, my dear, let us make you ready," said the fairy godmother. She waved her wand, and Cinderella's rags became a gorgeous ballgown of white silk and silver thread. Glass slippers appeared on her feet, and a necklace of pearls adorned her neck. She looked absolutely beautiful.

"Remember," warned the fairy godmother seriously, "the magic ends at midnight. The coach will become a pumpkin again, the horses will become mice, and your gown will become rags. You must leave the ball before the clock strikes twelve."

"I will remember," promised Cinderella.

When Cinderella arrived at the ball, everyone stared in wonder. Even the stepmother and stepsisters did not recognize her. The prince, seeing her, immediately forgot about all the other girls. He asked her to dance, and they danced together the entire evening.

They talked and laughed, and the prince found himself completely enchanted by this mysterious, beautiful girl. Cinderella was so happy, she almost forgot the fairy godmother's warning.

Suddenly, the clock began to strike midnight. Cinderella remembered the warning and gasped.

"I must go!" she cried, pulling away from the prince.

She ran from the ballroom and down the palace stairs. In her haste, one of her glass slippers fell off her foot. She had no time to retrieve it; the magic was fading. She reached the coach just as it turned back into a pumpkin, but she managed to escape before the transformation completed.

The prince, holding the single glass slipper, was determined to find his mysterious love. He announced that he would search every house in the kingdom until he found the girl whose foot fit the slipper.

When the prince came to Cinderella's house, the stepsisters eagerly tried on the slipper. Neither could fit it into the shoe, no matter how hard they tried.

"Is there anyone else in the house?" asked the prince.

"Only the servant girl," sneered the stepmother.

When Cinderella appeared, the prince recognized her immediately. The slipper fit her perfectly.

The prince knelt before her. "Will you marry me?" he asked.

With joy overflowing her heart, Cinderella said yes. They were married in a grand ceremony at the palace, and Cinderella left behind her life of hardship. She became a princess, loved and cherished by the prince and the entire kingdom. And though Cinderella was kind even to those who had treated her cruelly, everyone agreed that she had found the happiness she truly deserved.

B1.text:
In a prosperous household there once lived a gentle girl named Ella, who had been blessed with a comfortable life: a loving mother, an attentive father, and all the comforts that wealth could provide. Tragedy, however, struck unexpectedly when her mother fell gravely ill and departed this world, leaving Ella inconsolable. Her father, hoping to provide her with maternal guidance, remarried within a few years. His new wife was a woman of noble birth but possessed neither warmth nor kindness; her two daughters inherited only her coldness and vanity.

Following her father's untimely death, Ella's circumstances deteriorated dramatically. The stepmother, no longer constrained by her husband's presence, revealed her true nature. She stripped Ella of her rightful place and reduced her to servitude, forcing her to work as a common maid in her own home. While the stepsisters spent their days adorning themselves and pursuing frivolous pleasures, Ella labored ceaselessly, cooking meals, scrubbing floors, and mending clothes.

Because Ella frequently sat among the ashes of the kitchen hearth, her stepsisters mockingly renamed her "Cinderella." The nickname, cruel though it was, eventually eclipsed her real name in common usage. Cinderella bore her misfortune with remarkable grace, maintaining her gentle disposition despite the constant mistreatment she endured.

One momentous day, an announcement reached the household that shook the kingdom with excitement: the young prince was now of marriageable age, and the king had decreed a grand ball to be held at the palace. Every eligible maiden in the realm was invited to attend, for the prince would select his bride from among them. The stepmother's household erupted in chaos as the stepsisters scrambled to prepare themselves for this unprecedented opportunity.

The stepmother's cruelty intensified around this event. She made Cinderella work even harder, requiring her to prepare elaborate toilettes for the stepsisters while remaining at home herself. Cinderella's heart ached with longing, but she remained silent and obedient.

On the evening of the ball, after the stepmother and stepsisters departed in their carriage, Cinderella sat alone by the fire, weeping quietly. Then, without warning, a brilliant light flooded the kitchen, and an ethereal figure materialized before her—a woman of extraordinary elegance and wisdom.

"Why do you weep, my child?" asked the woman tenderly.

"I am your fairy godmother," she continued. "I shall ensure that you attend the ball this night."

Cinderella was amazed. "But how is this possible? I have no suitable gown, and no means of transportation."

The fairy godmother smiled. "Go to the garden and fetch me the largest pumpkin you can find."

When Cinderella returned with the pumpkin, the fairy godmother touched it with her wand, and it immediately transformed into an ornate golden coach of magnificent proportions. She then requested six mice from the pantry, which she likewise transformed into six elegant white horses.

"Now, my dear," said the fairy godmother, "let us attend to you."

With a wave of her wand, Cinderella's tattered rags became a spectacular ballgown of white silk interwoven with silver thread. Her feet were adorned with glass slippers, transparent and exquisite. A diamond necklace appeared at her throat, and her hair was arranged in an elegant coiffure.

"You are transformed, child," said the fairy godmother with satisfaction. "However, you must remember one crucial matter: the enchantment will fade at the stroke of midnight. Your coach will revert to a pumpkin, your horses to mice, and your gown to rags. You must depart the ball before the twelfth hour concludes."

"I understand," promised Cinderella. "I shall not forget."

When Cinderella arrived at the palace, an astonished silence fell over the assembly. The stepmother and stepsisters, recognizing no one they knew, were equally mystified by this breathtakingly beautiful stranger. The prince, however, recognized something indefinably precious in her bearing and immediately requested her hand in dance.

Throughout the evening, the prince danced only with Cinderella. Their conversation flowed naturally, touching upon subjects both trivial and profound. The prince found himself utterly captivated, having never encountered a maiden who possessed such grace, intelligence, and kindness simultaneously. Cinderella too found herself enchanted by his genuine warmth and genuine interest in her thoughts.

Lost in the pleasure of their companionship, Cinderella nearly failed to notice when the palace clock began to chime midnight. Suddenly remembering the fairy godmother's warning, she exclaimed in alarm and fled from the ballroom without explanation.

In her desperate haste to descend the palace staircase, one of her glass slippers slipped from her foot and remained on the steps. She could not stop to retrieve it; the magic was already dissolving. She reached the courtyard just in time to see her coach transform back into a pumpkin.

The prince, bewildered and heartbroken by her sudden disappearance, found the delicate glass slipper on the staircase. He held it as though it were the most precious object in existence.

"I shall find her," he declared with absolute resolve. "I will search every corner of this kingdom until I locate the maiden whose foot fits this slipper. She alone shall be my bride."

Beginning the very next day, the prince traveled from house to house throughout the kingdom, his servants preceding him with the glass slipper. Every unmarried woman was invited to attempt to fit her foot into the shoe, but none succeeded.

When the prince arrived at Cinderella's house, the stepsisters attempted the trial with great eagerness, but the slipper would not fit either of them. Their mother was desperate; she attempted various stratagems to make the shoe fit, but it remained stubbornly unchanged.

"Is there anyone else in this household?" asked the prince finally.

The stepmother dismissed the question dismissively. "Only a servant girl, but surely you do not mean to test the maid?"

The prince insisted, and Cinderella was summoned. Though she wore her customary tattered dress and her face bore the marks of her labor, the prince recognized her immediately. When she placed her foot in the slipper, it fit perfectly, as though fashioned specifically for her alone.

"You are the one I have searched for," breathed the prince, his eyes alight with joy and recognition. "Will you consent to marry me?"

With tears of happiness streaming down her face, Cinderella agreed. They were married in a ceremony of great splendor, and Cinderella ascended to her rightful place as the prince's bride. She left behind her life of servitude and hardship, exchanging it for a life of love, respect, and genuine happiness.

Moreover, Cinderella's kind heart proved true to her character. In time, she forgave her stepmother and stepsisters, using her influence as princess to secure them advantageous matches. Though her kindness to those who had mistreated her was perhaps excessive, all who knew her agreed that she had earned her happiness a thousand times over through her virtue and gentle spirit.

B2.text:
There once existed a maiden of considerable virtue and gentle temperament, whose name was Ella, though history would know her by an altogether different appellation. She had been born into circumstances of considerable comfort—a loving mother, a devoted father, and an estate of substantial prosperity. Yet Fortune, ever capricious in her dispensations, withdrew these blessings with merciless swiftness. Her mother's untimely demise left her bereft, and though her father sought to provide her with a mother's guidance through remarriage, this union proved catastrophic rather than redemptive.

The woman he married possessed beauty and social standing, but beneath these superficial attributes dwelt a heart as cold and barren as winter stone. Her two daughters, having inherited her mother's vanity and moral emptiness, regarded their new stepsister with contempt barely concealed beneath the thinnest veneer of civility. When Ella's father passed from this world—whether by natural causes or through grief that accelerated his decline—the stepmother's restraint evaporated entirely.

Elла was demoted from stepdaughter to drudge. The beautiful rooms in which she had been raised became forbidden to her; she slept in a cramped servant's chamber adjacent to the kitchen. Her elegant wardrobe was confiscated and replaced with threadbare garments. What had once been her father's household became a gilded prison, and she was its prisoner. Her days were consumed in unending labor: preparing meals for those who scorned her, scrubbing floors that never seemed to remain clean, and mending the elaborate garments her stepsisters carelessly damaged.

Yet Ella bore these indignities without bitterness, maintaining an equanimity and graciousness that seemed to transcend the circumstances of her degradation. She was often observed sitting by the kitchen fireplace, her face illuminated by the flickering flames, the ashes from the hearth settling upon her dress like some perverse cosmetic. It was from this image that her cruel nickname derived: "Cinderella," a diminishment that seemed to accumulate moral weight with each repetition. Years accumulated in this servitude, and Cinderella became, to the world, less a person than a fixture—a piece of furniture whose function was to serve the comfort of others.

Then came the news that shifted the entire kingdom's attention: the prince, heir to the throne and now of an age to marry, would select his bride from among all eligible maidens in the realm. The king decreed a grand ball to be held at the palace, where the prince would observe the assembled young women and choose his future queen. This announcement arrived at Cinderella's household like a thunderbolt, electrifying the stepmother and her daughters into a frenzy of preparation and self-improvement.

The stepmother, recognizing that this event represented an opportunity to elevate her daughters' status—and consequently her own—spared no expense in their adornment. Vast sums were invested in the finest fabrics, the most accomplished seamstresses, and the most fashionable coiffures. The stepsisters, already predisposed toward vanity, became consumed by it entirely, spending entire days examining their reflections and critiquing their appearance with the intensity of serious scholars.

Meanwhile, Cinderella was pressed into service with even greater demands. She was required not merely to complete her usual tasks but also to dress the stepsisters' hair, to arrange their gowns, and to attend to their every whim. When she ventured to express a desire to attend the ball herself, the stepmother's response was to mock her and to assign her an impossible task: to sort a large pile of lentils from ashes, implying that only through the completion of this absurd task might she attend. Knowing the task to be deliberately designed as impossible, Cinderella gathered her courage, and with the assistance of some birds attracted by the breadcrumbs she scattered, she actually managed to complete it. The stepmother, furious that her stratagem had failed, invented a new excuse: Cinderella possessed no appropriate dress and no means of transportation, and therefore could not possibly attend.

On the evening of the ball, the stepmother and stepsisters departed in their carriage, leaving Cinderella alone in the kitchen. She sat by the fire, her heart heavy with disappointment, and allowed herself to weep quietly. But as the shadows lengthened and twilight deepened into evening, the kitchen was suddenly suffused with an otherworldly light, and a figure of transcendent beauty materialized before her.

"Why do you weep, my child?" inquired the apparition. "I am your fairy godmother, summoned by your tears and your virtuous heart. I shall not permit your stepmother's cruelty to deprive you of this night's joy."

Cinderella's astonishment was profound, but the fairy godmother permitted no time for questions. She instructed Cinderella to fetch a pumpkin from the garden. When Cinderella returned, the fairy godmother touched it with her wand, and it metamorphosed into a coach of genuine magnificence—all gilt wood and crystal windows, with plush velvet upholstery within. She then requested six mice, which Cinderella readily provided. Each mouse, at the touch of the wand, transformed into a spirited white horse, perfectly matched and fitted with silver harnesses.

"But I am still unfit to attend," protested Cinderella, gesturing to her tattered dress.

The fairy godmother smiled and waved her wand once more. Cinderella's garments dissolved, and in their place emerged a ballgown of incomparable beauty—white silk so fine it seemed almost ethereal, interwoven with thread of silver that caught the light like captured starlight. The neckline was modest yet elegant, and the skirt flowed in graceful layers. Upon her feet appeared slippers fashioned from pure glass, transparent and delicate, as though spun from the dreams of master craftsmen. A tiara of small diamonds was set upon her head, and about her throat lay a single strand of luminous pearls.

"You are transformed," said the fairy godmother with satisfaction. "But hear me well: this enchantment is bound by time. When the clock in the palace tower strikes the twelfth hour—at midnight—the magic will dissolve entirely. Your coach will revert to a pumpkin, your horses to mice, your gown to rags, and these slippers to nothing. You must depart the ball before the final chime ceases to echo."

"I shall not forget," promised Cinderella solemnly.

When Cinderella arrived at the palace, descending from her pumpkin-coach with practiced grace, she created a sensation beyond measure. The assembled nobility, accustomed to the studied elegance of the realm's most prominent families, found themselves entirely outshone. Even the stepmother and stepsisters, positioned among the throng, failed to recognize her, though they felt a vague inexplicable resentment at the attention the stranger commanded.

But it was the prince whose reaction proved most profound. He had dutifully danced with various maidens throughout the evening, fulfilling his duty as heir, but had found none who engaged his genuine interest. When he perceived Cinderella, however, everything altered. He abandoned his customary reserve and approached her directly.

"May I have the honor of this dance?" he inquired, his voice betraying an uncharacteristic intensity.

With characteristic grace, Cinderella accepted. They danced together throughout the evening, and as they did, a conversation evolved that touched upon subjects both profound and delightful. The prince discovered in her a mind of considerable acuity, a humor both sharp and kind, and a perspective on life that transcended the superficiality he had previously encountered. Cinderella, in turn, found in the prince a genuine humanity—an absence of pretension and a capacity for authentic connection that moved her profoundly.

So absorbed were they in each other's company that Cinderella nearly failed to notice when the palace clock began its midnight announcement. The first chime jolted her from her reverie, and she abruptly became aware that her enchanted hours were expiring.

"Forgive me, I must go!" she cried, pulling away from the prince's embrace.

Before he could respond or inquire into her sudden distress, she fled from the ballroom. In her desperate haste to descend the palace's grand staircase, her left foot slipped, and one glass slipper remained behind on the steps. She could not return for it; already her gown was beginning to lose its luster, and she could feel the magic unraveling. She reached the courtyard moments before the final chime sounded, and watched as her coach reverted to a pumpkin, her horses to mice. She found herself standing in the street in tattered clothes, clutching the single remaining glass slipper that had somehow survived the dissolution of the spell.

The prince, devastated by her mysterious departure, retrieved the slipper from the stairs and examined it with fascination. Its delicate craftsmanship suggested that whoever had worn it possessed both grace and refinement. He held it before him like a talisman.

"I shall find her," he declared, his voice resonant with absolute conviction. "I will search every dwelling in this kingdom if necessary. She alone shall be my bride, for I know with certainty that our destinies are intertwined."

Beginning at dawn, the prince and his attendants undertook their search. They carried the slipper from household to household, inviting every unmarried woman to attempt to fit her foot within it. But the slipper, seemingly enchanted itself, would not accommodate any foot save one. Some maidens attempted to force their feet into it, causing themselves pain; others wept with frustration at their inability to match it. Yet none succeeded.

When the prince's entourage arrived at Cinderella's household, the stepmother's countenance transformed from casual indifference to desperate ambition. The stepsisters, though they privately doubted success, competed with vicious enthusiasm to fit their feet into the slipper. Their mother, observing their failure, resorted to desperate measures—applying salves, attempting to stretch the slipper, and even suggesting it might be improperly sized—but no stratagem could overcome the fundamental incompatibility.

"Is there no other woman in this household?" inquired the prince, his patience beginning to fray.

The stepmother, her face flushed with anger and shame, gestured dismissively toward the kitchen. "Only a servant girl, but surely—"

The prince's eyes flashed with a determination that brooked no contradiction. "I insist upon testing every woman in this kingdom, regardless of her station."

When Cinderella emerged from the kitchen in her customary tattered dress, her face bearing the marks of her labors, the stepsisters emitted gasps of outrage. Yet the prince's recognition was immediate and absolute. Though her circumstances had altered dramatically, the essential quality that had captivated him—some ineffable combination of grace, kindness, and genuine beauty—remained unchanged.

"May I?" he asked gently, kneeling before her.

As Cinderella extended her foot, the slipper settled upon it with perfect precision, as though it had been fashioned specifically for her and no other. Its complement, which Cinderella produced from the depths of her pocket, was then placed upon her other foot, completing the transformation. In that moment, the simple peasant dress she wore seemed to transform, and Cinderella stood revealed in her true nature—no servant, but a maiden of extraordinary worth.

"It is you," breathed the prince. "I have searched for you with every breath since you departed. Will you consent to marry me and become my princess?"

With tears of joy and relief streaming down her face—tears that seemed to wash away not merely the dirt of her servitude but all the accumulated sorrow of her years of suffering—Cinderella accepted. They were married in a ceremony of extraordinary magnificence, attended by nobility from throughout the kingdom and celebrated with festivities that lasted for weeks.

Yet Cinderella's virtuous nature did not permit her to harbor bitterness even toward those who had abused her. In the years that followed, she used her position and influence to secure advantageous marriages for her stepsisters and to provide her stepmother with a comfortable income sufficient for her maintenance. Though some observers found her generosity to those who had treated her so cruelly to be excessive, all agreed that she had earned her happiness through virtue and grace, and that no fate could have been more just or more deserved.
